title: Critical Thinking and Logical Reasoning
summary: Learn to judge claims, spot weak arguments and misinformation, notice your own biases, and make well-reasoned decisions.

body.p: A claim is a statement that says something is true. 'The school library is open until 5 pm' is a claim. So is 'Homework makes students cleverer'. Some claims can be checked quickly, such as the library hours. Others need evidence, which means facts, measurements, examples or expert knowledge that give us a reason to believe the claim. A claim with no evidence is only an opinion, and an opinion is not wrong for that reason, but it should not convince you until you see support for it.

In everyday speech an argument means a quarrel. In critical thinking an argument is a set of reasons that support a conclusion. The reasons are called premises. The conclusion is the claim the premises are meant to prove. Words such as 'because', 'since', 'so', 'therefore' and 'it follows that' often point to them.

body.code:
Premise 1: Every student who passed the practical test attended the revision classes.
Premise 2: Ngozi passed the practical test.
Conclusion: Ngozi attended the revision classes.

body.p: Here, if both premises are true, the conclusion must be true. We call this a valid argument. Validity is about the shape of the reasoning, not about whether the premises are true. Compare this one: 'All birds can swim. A hen is a bird. So a hen can swim.' The shape is valid, but the first premise is false, so the argument is not sound. A sound argument is valid AND has true premises.

steps: Find the conclusion: what is the writer trying to make you believe?
List the premises: what reasons are given? Add any hidden premise the writer is assuming.
Ask: are the premises true, and what evidence is given for each?
Ask: if the premises are true, does the conclusion really follow, or could it be false?
Decide how strongly you believe the conclusion: fully, partly or not yet.

body.p: Kwame says: 'Our school should start at 9 am instead of 8 am, because teenagers need more sleep, and students who sleep more concentrate better.' The conclusion is that the school should start at 9 am. The premises are that teenagers need more sleep and that more sleep improves concentration. A hidden premise is that a later start will actually give students more sleep rather than just making them go to bed later. A careful thinker accepts the two stated premises as plausible but asks for evidence about the hidden one. The argument is reasonable, but not yet proven.

body.tip: When you meet a strong claim, ask three quick questions: What exactly is being claimed? What is the evidence? Could something else explain it?

body.p: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning that makes an argument look stronger than it is. Fallacies are common in adverts, social media, playground debates and even classroom discussions. Learning their names helps you notice them. Remember that a fallacy shows the argument is weak; it does not prove the conclusion is false. The conclusion might still be true for other reasons.

list: Ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument. 'Tunde says we should recycle bottles, but he is always late, so ignore him.' His punctuality has nothing to do with whether recycling is useful.

Straw man: twisting someone's view into a weaker version and attacking that. A says, 'We should have less homework on weekends.' B replies, 'So you want no homework at all and no learning!' A never said that.
False dilemma: offering only two choices when more exist. 'Either you join the football team or you do not care about school.' There are many other possibilities.
Slippery slope: claiming one small step will inevitably lead to a disaster, without evidence. 'If we let phones in class today, soon nobody will study at all.'
Appeal to popularity: 'Everyone is buying this drink, so it must be healthy.' Many people believing something does not make it true.
Hasty generalisation: concluding about a whole group from too few or unusual examples.
Post hoc (after this, therefore because of this): assuming that because B followed A, A caused B.

body.h: Worked examples: hasty generalisation and post hoc

body.p: Imagine you ask 5 classmates about a new canteen menu and 3 say they dislike it. That is 60 percent of the people you asked, which sounds like a lot. But if your school has 1200 students, you have asked only 0.4 percent of them. Saying 'most students hate the menu' from 5 answers is a hasty generalisation. A bigger and fairer sample, such as students from every year group chosen at random, would be stronger evidence.

For post hoc: Ada wears her green socks to a test and scores well. She concludes that the socks caused the good mark. But she also revised for a week. Two things happening one after the other does not show that one caused the other. To claim cause you need to rule out other explanations and, ideally, compare cases with and without the supposed cause.

body.tip: When you spot a fallacy, say it kindly: 'That is one example, can we find more?' works better than shouting 'Fallacy!'.

body.p: Fallacies are mistakes in arguments. Cognitive biases are habits of the mind that push all of us, including clever people, towards certain errors. They are not signs of stupidity. They are shortcuts that usually save time but sometimes lead us wrong. You cannot remove them completely, but you can slow down and check yourself.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for, notice and remember information that supports what we already believe, and to ignore or explain away information that does not. Suppose Chidi believes he is 'bad at Chemistry'. He remembers every low mark and forgets the two good ones. When he gets a good mark he says it was luck. His belief never gets challenged, so it never changes. The same happens when we only follow online accounts that agree with us.
A simple remedy is to search on purpose for the opposite view. Ask, 'What would I expect to see if I were wrong?' and then look for it honestly.

Anchoring is when the first number or idea we hear has too much influence on our judgment. A market trader says a bag costs 5,000 in local currency, then offers it for 3,000. The 3,000 feels like a bargain because of the first figure, even if the bag is worth only 2,000. The same happens with exam marks: if your first test score was very low, you may 'anchor' on it and underestimate your later ability.

list: Pause before reacting to a claim that makes you feel strongly angry or pleased.
Find out the usual or fair value of something before hearing the seller's number.
Write down your prediction before you see a result, so you cannot pretend later that you expected it.
Ask a friend who disagrees with you to explain their reasoning, and listen to the whole answer.

body.tip: Feeling certain is not the same as being right. Strong feelings are a good signal to check the evidence once more.

body.p: Misinformation is false or misleading information, often shared by people who believe it and mean no harm. Disinformation is false information shared on purpose to mislead. Both spread fast on phones because a message arrives from a friend, so it feels trustworthy. Before you share, forward or believe something, take a few minutes to check.

steps: Stop. Notice your reaction. Messages that make you shocked or afraid are designed to be shared quickly.
Who made it? Look for a named author or organisation. 'Forwarded as received' is not a source.
What is the evidence? Is there a link to original data, a report or a named expert, or only strong words?
When was it published? Old news is often recirculated as if it were new.
Can you find the same claim from two or more independent and reliable sources, such as a national statistics office, a university, an established news organisation or a school exam board?
Check images: search for the picture to see whether it comes from a different event or year.

body.p: A message says: 'URGENT! Drinking hot water with lemon stops all exam stress. Doctors confirm. Share with 10 friends!' Check it. 'Doctors' are not named. No study is given. The message demands you share it, which is a pressure tactic. 'All' is an absolute claim that real science rarely makes. A search finds no health authority supporting it. The sensible conclusion is that the claim is unsupported. Warm drinks may feel comforting, but that is different from 'stops all stress'.

Now compare it with a school exam board posting a timetable change on its own official website with a date, a contact address and a notice number. The source is named, accountable and directly in charge of the information. It is much stronger evidence, though you can still confirm it by asking your teacher.

body.tip: Headlines are written to attract clicks. Always read beyond the headline before deciding what a story claims.

body.p: A strong argument does not pretend that only one side exists. It states a clear position, supports it with good reasons, and then deals fairly with the best opposing view. This is called a balanced argument, and it is what teachers and examiners reward in essays, debates and discussion questions.

steps: State the question neutrally, for example: 'Should students be allowed to use calculators in all Mathematics lessons?'
Make your position clear in one sentence: 'Calculators should be allowed for most lessons, but not for learning basic number facts.'
Give two or three reasons, each with evidence or an example.
State the strongest opposing argument fairly, in words its supporters would accept. This avoids a straw man.
Reply to it: explain why it does not change your view, or admit where it does and adjust your position.
Conclude, saying how confident you are and what further evidence could change your mind.

body.code:
Position: Schools should provide a short break between lessons.
Reason 1: Short breaks let students rest, which supports concentration (give a source or a class example).
Reason 2: Students can move and drink water, which helps the afternoon lessons.
Opposing view: Breaks cut teaching time, which could hurt syllabus coverage.
Reply: Breaks of five minutes cost little time, and a tired class often learns less in the remaining time anyway. A trial of one term could test this.

body.p: Notice what this writer did. The opposing view is stated fairly. The reply does not insult anyone. The ending suggests a way to test the idea with evidence. That is stronger than 'Breaks are good and anyone who disagrees is lazy', which would be an ad hominem.

list: Have I used any fallacy from the list, such as a false dilemma?
Is each reason backed by evidence rather than just opinion?
Have I used words like 'always', 'never' and 'everyone' when 'often' or 'many' is more accurate?
Would someone who disagrees say I described their view fairly?

body.tip: Changing your mind when the evidence changes is a strength, not a weakness.

lessons.title: Making decisions with pros, cons and evidence

body.p: Critical thinking is not only for essays. You also use it for real choices, like which subjects to take, which course to apply for, or how to spend limited money. A list of pros and cons is a good start, but it works better when you add weights and evidence.

steps: Write the decision as a question: 'Which senior-school subject combination should I choose?'
List realistic options, including 'do nothing' or 'wait'.
For each option, list pros and cons. Be honest, not only hopeful.
Rate each pro or con from 1 (small) to 3 (big) for how much it matters to your goals.
For each point, note the evidence: a fact, a teacher's advice, a past mark or a published entry requirement. Mark opinions as opinions.
Add up the weights, but treat the total as a guide, not an order. Then sleep on it and talk to someone you trust.

body.p: Funmi must choose between Option A (Biology, Chemistry, Physics) and Option B (Biology, Chemistry, Geography). She wants to study nursing. Evidence from the university prospectus she has read: the course requires Biology and Chemistry, and accepts Physics or another science subject. Her last two Physics marks were weak, but her Geography marks are strong. Option B has the pros of better predicted marks and lower stress. The con is that she must check that Geography counts as an accepted subject. Option A has the pro of safer entry, but a risk to her final marks. Instead of deciding on feelings, Funmi's next step is to phone the admissions office and check the requirement. Good decisions often need one more fact before you choose.

list: Anchoring: do not choose only because the first option you heard sounded good.
Confirmation bias: look for reasons the option might fail.
Popularity: 'my friends are all taking it' is not enough evidence.
False dilemma: ask whether there is a third option, such as a combined or later route.

body.tip: A good decision made with the information available is still good even if luck later makes it turn out badly. Judge the thinking, not only the result.

quiz.q: A student writes: 'Because the new teacher is young, her advice on exam technique must be useless.' Which fallacy is this?
options: Ad hominem
Slippery slope
Post hoc
False dilemma

quiz.q: Sade says: 'We should have a shorter school assembly.' Her friend replies: 'So you think school assembly is worthless and we should cancel everything!' What has her friend done?
options: Made a hasty generalisation from a single example
Created a straw man by exaggerating Sade's actual view
Made an appeal to popularity about what most pupils want
Anchored on the first number that Sade mentioned

quiz.q: A poster says: 'Either you buy our revision guide or you will fail your exams.' What is the main flaw?
options: Ad hominem attack on the reader's intelligence and effort
Post hoc reasoning about the results of past students
False dilemma: there are other ways to prepare for exams
Confirmation bias on the part of the people who wrote it

quiz.q: After Musa began drinking a new fruit juice, his football performance improved. He says the juice caused it. He had also started training twice a week. What is the best response?
options: The juice caused it, because the improvement came after he started drinking it
The juice works, because many other players in the league drink it as well
Training did not matter, because the juice is the more recent change in his routine
He cannot tell the juice caused it because training is another possible explanation

quiz.q: Which of these is a valid argument?
options: All nurses in the clinic wear badges. Ama is a nurse there. So Ama wears a badge.
Some students like Maths. Kofi is a student. So Kofi must like Maths too.
The bus was late on Monday and again on Tuesday. So buses are always late.
Everyone in the school says it is true, so it must be true for all of us.

quiz.q: A survey asked 5 students about the school bus and 3 disliked it. The writer concludes that most students dislike the bus. What is wrong?
options: The writer attacked the students personally for their views
The sample of five is too small to speak for all students
The writer offered a false choice between two options only
The writer used a slippery slope with an unlikely chain

quiz.q: Ifeanyi believes he is poor at essay writing. He remembers every critical comment and forgets every compliment. Which bias is at work?
options: Anchoring
Appeal to popularity
Confirmation bias
Straw man

quiz.q: A seller says a phone costs 90,000, then 'reduces' it to 70,000. You decide it is a bargain without checking other prices. Which bias has influenced you?
options: Confirmation bias about the shop
Post hoc reasoning about the price
Ad hominem towards the shop owner
Anchoring on the first price he saw

quiz.q: A forwarded message says 'Experts say this app steals your marks. Share now!' with no names, no link and no date. What is the best first step?
options: Look for the original source and whether reliable organisations report the same thing
Forward it to your contacts in case it is true, so that they can protect their marks
Delete it at once and assume the opposite of what it says is the truth
Believe it because it came from a friend you trust and have known for years

quiz.q: Which source is strongest for the claim 'The national exam will start on 5 May'?
options: A classmate who says he heard it from someone in a higher class
The official exam board website, which names the date and a contact
An unsigned post with thousands of likes and many comments agreeing
A video with a dramatic title and a presenter who sounds very sure

quiz.q: Which sentence best states the opposing view fairly in a balanced essay on school uniforms?
options: People who support uniforms mostly like boring clothes and dislike self-expression.
Uniforms are for people who cannot think for themselves or make their own choices.
Supporters say uniforms reduce pressure to compete over clothes and make mornings simpler.
Most people know uniforms are pointless, so supporters rarely have a sensible reason.

quiz.q: A student says: 'If we allow one late assignment, soon nobody will hand work in on time and the school will collapse.' What is the problem?
options: It is an ad hominem, because it attacks the character of students
It is a valid argument, because each step follows from the last
It is an appeal to popularity, because it relies on what most people do
It is a slippery slope with no evidence for the chain of events

quiz.q: Chinwe is choosing between two courses. Which action shows the best critical thinking?
options: Check the entry requirements and her past marks for each course, then compare pros and cons
Choose the course her friends chose, so that she can study alongside people she knows
Choose the first course she heard about, since early information is usually the most reliable
Choose the one that feels more exciting today, ignoring requirements and her past marks
It has at least three premises supporting the conclusion
It has a valid structure and all of its premises are true
It is expressed confidently by a person with experience
Most people who hear it agree that it is reasonable

quiz.q: An advert says: 'Nine out of ten people love this snack!' but does not say who was asked. What should you do?
options: Accept it because nine out of ten is a large share
Reject it because adverts always lie, whatever figures they quote
Ask who was asked, how many, and how, before trusting it
Buy it because a snack that is this popular must be good

quiz.q: Which statement shows the best attitude when new evidence contradicts your view?
options: I will ignore it because I have thought about this for years
I will look only for other evidence that agrees with my view
I will attack the character of the person who found it
I will reconsider my position in light of the new evidence
